Neonatal mass in the Shining bronze cuckoo (Chalcites lucidus) is remarkably low, with newly hatched chicks weighing approximately 1.4 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.4 grams], a value consistent with the extreme altriciality and brood-parasitic lifestyle typical of many Cuculinae. This diminutive initial mass places a heavy premium on accelerated early growth, as the nestling must compete aggressively for parental provisioning from its often much smaller host parents. Field observations suggest that eggs incubated at the typical host nest temperature of 36.2 °C [T = 36.2 °C] complete development in about 11 days [ab = about 11 days], a notably short incubation period that facilitates rapid hatching ahead of or in synchrony with the host's own brood. The cuckoo chick's precocious hatching and subsequent eviction behavior are thus underpinned by a compressed embryonic development schedule that is tightly linked to the thermal environment of the host nest. This rapid transition from egg to feeding nestling represents a critical phase of the species' life cycle, during which the chick's competitive advantage is established.

Following the rapid hatching and eviction of host eggs, the surviving nestling enters a phase of intense somatic growth. Adults of this species ultimately attain an asymptotic body mass of 22 grams [Wwi = 22 grams], a modest size that positions the Shining bronze cuckoo among the smaller members of its genus. Achieving this adult mass requires a sustained high intake of arthropod prey delivered by the foster parents. The fledging stage, marking the point at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight, occurs approximately 19 days after hatching [tx = approximately 19 days after hatching], a developmental milestone reached under the elevated body temperatures characteristic of active endothermy, typically around 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This rapid transition from a 1.4-gram neonate (1.4 grams) [Wwb = 1.4 grams] to a volant juvenile capable of independent movement in roughly three weeks is an adaptive response to the risks of detection and predation within the host's nest. The energetic demands of this growth spurt are substantial, requiring the host parents to maintain a high provisioning rate to support the cuckoo chick's development.

Reproductive maturation in the Shining bronze cuckoo follows a distinct temporal progression. The onset of puberty, marked by the development of functional gonads and reproductive tract maturation, is reached at approximately 57 days after hatching [tp = approximately 57 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This physiological milestone occurs while the young bird's core temperature is regulated at roughly 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the typical active metabolic temperature for this species. However, the transition to actual breeding behavior is considerably more protracted; first successful reproduction, involving the location of a suitable host nest and the deposition of a single egg, typically occurs at about 365 days after hatching [tR = about 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This one-year delay between achieving sexual maturity and initiating reproductive activity likely reflects the time required for young birds to acquire the necessary spatial knowledge of host territories, refine their egg-mimicry laying behavior, and establish themselves within the local breeding population. The first brood episode is thus a landmark event in an individual's life history.

The longevity and lifetime reproductive output of the Shining bronze cuckoo are constrained by its brood-parasitic strategy. Maximum recorded lifespan in the wild is approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years], a considerable duration for a bird of its body mass, likely facilitated by a relatively low adult mortality rate once individuals reac at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]h breeding age. This per-event fixed output of one egg per host nest [N_R_i = one egg per host nest] reflects the behavioral limitation of laying a single egg per available nest. When integrated over a 15-year (15 years) [am = 15 years] lifespan, a single female can produce a substantial number of offspring across multiple breeding seasons at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. The species thus employs a strategy of high adult survival and low per-event fecundity, contrasting strongly with many non-parasitic passerines that produce larger clutches annually.

Under the temperature conditions typical of this species during active periods (41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]), the inter-breeding interval and developmental schedules are optimized for a parasitic lifestyle. The annual reproductive cycle, with first breeding occurring at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], effectively synchronizes the cuckoo's laying season with that of its primary hosts at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. For those individuals that survive to the maximum recorded lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years], the cumulative breeding opportunities are substantial, with a single egg laid per clutch [N_R_i = single egg laid per clutch] per parasitized nest representing a lifetime investment spread across many host breeding attempts at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. Comparative data from related Chrysococcyx species suggest that this blend of extended longevity, delayed first reproduction, and low per-clutch output is a common life-history syndrome among obligate brood parasites. The physiological regulation of these life-history traits at a body temperature of 41.3 °C underscores the high metabolic demands of sustained flight and territorial patrolling required for successful host location and parasitism.
